note: Waya is pronounced Why-a, and Unole is pronounces OO-nol-lay

Just a few miles west of Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the gently rolling hills were left barren of trees from the large ranches that used to be there. The two year drought stripped the grass of its greenery, leaving only scarce bits of straw and a few rattlesnakes curled up in the prickly, dried, autumn earth. Tahlequah held up better in those days, saved by the large glittering lakes and plentiful streams; the heavily treed area hardly noticed the growing patch of sun burnt earth growing ever closer. That fall seemed more dead than the other years prior.

Carter took a long swig from his canteen, pouring some of the liquid out to a dish for his faithful companion, Waya. Waya lapped up the water, splashing it unintentionally on her fur. She shook her large head, the water splaying in different directions. Carter sighed, looking around. Still morning, the air had a chill on it. Soon, the sun would rise and by noon, he figured it'd be about 80 degrees. A hellish winter would follow. As he glanced around for any sign of life, he patted his trusted horse, Unole.

Unole, about 9 years old, had been in Carter's capable hands for eight years now. He was a tough one, but fast and sturdy- worth the hassle to train. Carter took off some of the pack from his saddle, allowing Unole to rest for a moment. Waya sniffed the crisp, new autumn breeze, the rising sun catching her hair in its bright rays of light. Cart slowly chewed on tobacco, spitting to the ground every so often, looking for a sign. A mark. Anything.

The hard dirt hardly told a secret. But Carter knew how to look, how to sense.

Grass folded in a certain pattern, dust kicked up. The man he was tracking was headed southwest, to Muskogee.

Guys, I'm taking a break from story telling. I'm going to use this prompt as a sort of Story into my own mind, away from characters. I hope you're okay with that. This picture brought back some visions of home and made me think about things that I can't attach to a character, just myself. Long story short, I miss having a home, and am going to reflect upon that here.

Emotionally, I'm lost. I have ideas of where I should go, and what I should do, but overall, I'm a walking disaster.

When I lived in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, I was a different person. I was 8 years old. My mother and father left me with my Aunt while my mother went to chemotherapy and my father served deployment in Bosnia. My mother always treated me as though I'd break when I stepped outside. For years I thought there was something wrong with me, but when I got to Oklahoma, suddenly I was free.

I got to spend time on my Granny's ranch, training the horses. I got to feed the ducks, muck stalls, teach ducks to swim... it was an amazing time. When I was at the ranch, I forgot that my mother could die any moment, I forgot that I was supposed to be sick and really just lived. This was the first time I felt alive.

We moved to Kansas. My dad was back, my mother survived for the time being (she'd later die of brain cancer). I was back to being "sickly" and "fragile" as my mother put it. I think she was projecting. I delved deeply into art. But that's not the story, just some background.

Right now, at 25, I'm living in a state where I feel no connectivity to the earth. I went back to Oklahoma a couple of years ago, and it may be the Cherokee in me, but every time I'm there, I feel a little pulse in the earth. A hum, like some kind of energy is floating up from under my feet and all of my anxiety goes away. But I'm back in the other state now. And there's nothing. Just dead concrete under my shoes and no life. Oklahoma and Kansas were different. I was different there. I could touch the ground and feel some sort of emotion that made my anxiety disappear. Like there was life in a world of death.

I miss feeling that. I am so lost here, I feel nothing with the earth. I feel like it's not fertile. The vegetables tasted better there, but here just cold and flavorless. The soil doesn't smell right. The air is thick and I can't breathe correctly. Back in Oklahoma, in Kansas, the air felt good. The soil smelled right, there was life all around me, just popping up and I wasn't afraid.

But here I'm scared. Nothing sits right. No heartbeat, no rhythmic pulse of the grass under my feet. Just.... stillness. And anxiety. I don't feel like this place is home. There is no place I'd rather be than a large open field where I can feel the ground pulsating under my small, childish feet. This place makes me afraid.

I want to go home. I want to find home. I Don't think it's Oklahoma. The people there are too stuck up and revolved around jesus. But I think if I felt that energy again, I might just be okay. The reservation and the highly native areas were pleasant. Everyone was so kind. They explained to me the feelings.

I don't have papers. I can't live on the reservation. my grandfather burned the papers. I don't know why. We're unofficially tribes people now.

I want to go home. But as of now, I can't find where home is.

Sorry again. This prompt is frustrating, because it so encapsulates what I want home to be. My dad is half cherokee, but we're not a part of the tribe. This prompt kind of hit home with me. I used to have a horse similar looking, and I would always stare at the ground trying to find tracks.
